title: How the Printing Press Changed the World
paragraphs: Until the mid-fifteenth century, every book in Europe was the product of painstaking manual labour. Scribes, many of them monks, could spend months copying a single manuscript, and errors inevitably crept in with each new copy. Books were therefore rare, expensive and concentrated in the hands of religious institutions, universities and the aristocracy.

Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith working in Mainz, transformed this situation not through a single invention but through an ingenious combination of techniques. He cast durable movable type from a metal alloy, devised an oil-based ink that adhered to metal, and adapted the screw press long used in winemaking. The result was a system in which pages could be composed, printed in large numbers and broken down again for reuse.

The impact was remarkably swift. The so-called Gutenberg Bible, completed around 1455, demonstrated that mechanically produced books could rival manuscripts in quality. Within half a century, presses were operating in hundreds of European towns, and the number of books in circulation had grown by orders of magnitude, while their cost had plummeted.

The consequences extended far beyond the book trade. Wider access to texts fostered literacy and created a reading public; inexpensive pamphlets enabled reformers such as Martin Luther to reach audiences on an unprecedented scale; and standardised editions allowed scholars to compare, correct and build upon one another’s work. It is no exaggeration to say that the press helped make the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and, ultimately, modern mass communication possible.
